passage:
Monday. "Did you submit the science model?" Sunaina didi asked at dinner. "Yes," Suraj said, not looking up. He had not even started it.
Wednesday. Didi met his science teacher at the vegetable market and came home with a face like thunder. "Ma'am says there was no model from you."
Suraj's heart hammered. Words came out before he could stop them. "She lost it. She loses everyone's things." Didi just looked at him. So he went louder. "Why are you even talking to my teachers? Are you spying on me now?" He slammed his door so hard the calendar fell off the wall.
Friday. He hadn't slept properly for two nights. Every time he pictured Ma'am's face on Monday, he felt sick. The second lie was worse than the first, and the shouting was worse than both.
That evening he knocked on Didi's door. "I never made it," he said. "Not even started. I'm sorry I yelled."

qa.q: What fell off the wall when Suraj slammed the door?
qa.a: The calendar fell off the wall.

qa.q: Why did Suraj blame the teacher and shout at Didi on Wednesday?
qa.a: Suraj panicked when caught and felt deep shame, so his mind grabbed for escape with a second lie and an attack instead of admitting it.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Suraj, and what did he do?
qa.a: Two sleepless nights of dreading Monday made him see the second lie and the shouting were worse, so on Friday he admitted the truth to Didi and apologised.

qa.q: How might Sunaina didi have felt when Suraj accused her of spying?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and wrongly blamed, since she had only asked and then learned the truth by chance.

grounding: Over a week, a teenage boy caught in a lie adds another and attacks his sister in panic and shame, before finally admitting it.

passage:
Varun, you think you're the first boy to be caught lying and dig the hole deeper? Sit. Your Deepak Chacha did it better.
I was fourteen. I cracked Mrs Sequeira's window with a cricket ball. When Amma asked, I said it was Salim from the next lane. Just like that.
Amma looked at me. "Salim was at his Nani's in Pune all week."
My ears went hot. I said, "Then it was his cousin." Now I had two lies. When Amma didn't answer, I shouted, "You always believe everyone except me!" and ran to the terrace.
I sat up there till dark, feeling like I'd swallowed a stone. I had called Salim a liar in my head just to escape.
At night, Amma came up with two glasses of milk and just sat. After a while I said, "It was me. Salim didn't do anything."
"I know," she said. "Now we go to Mrs Sequeira tomorrow."

qa.q: Where was Salim all week, according to Amma?
qa.a: Amma said Salim was at his Nani's in Pune all week.

qa.q: What was young Deepak feeling up on the terrace?
qa.a: Deepak felt heavy shame, like he'd swallowed a stone, knowing he had blamed Salim and shouted just to escape.

qa.q: Which moment in the story let young Deepak finally tell the truth?
qa.a: Amma coming up with two glasses of milk and sitting quietly, without anger, gave Deepak the space to admit it was him.

qa.q: How might Salim have been affected if Deepak's lie had stuck?
qa.a: Salim could have been blamed and punished for a window he never touched, just because Deepak panicked.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fourteen, he panicked when caught, added a second lie and attacked his mother, before shame led him to admit it.

passage:
At the Saturday fair in Rajgarh, Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition. Now her cousin Mahima was standing at the bangle stall, looking right at her.
"Jyoti? Aren't you supposed to be at Sharma sir's?"
Jyoti's face went hot. "Tuition got cancelled. Sir had a wedding."
"I just saw Sharma sir at the tea stall. He said class was on."
"He's lying. He always forgets." The words tumbled out. "And why are you spying on me? You're always trying to get me in trouble, didi!"
Mahima blinked. "I'm not spying. I came for bangles."
Jyoti turned and walked fast through the crowd, heart thumping, the lie getting heavier with every step. By the time she reached the Ferris wheel she wanted to cry. She had called her favourite teacher a liar and her favourite cousin a spy, all to avoid saying one true sentence.

qa.q: What had Jyoti told her mother about Saturday?
qa.a: Jyoti had told her mother she was at tuition.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti call Mahima a spy?
qa.a: Jyoti panicked and felt ashamed at being caught, so attacking Mahima felt easier than admitting the truth.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do now to stop the lies piling up?
qa.a: Go back to Mahima, admit she skipped tuition, apologise for calling her a spy, and tell her mother herself that evening.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel after being called a spy?
qa.a: Mahima was confused and probably hurt, since she had only come for bangles and was suddenly treated as an enemy.

grounding: Shows a teenager caught in a lie adding new lies and attacking the cousin who found out, because shame makes escape feel easier than admission.

passage:
In the family's flat in Amman, Layla opened the shared laptop to print her CV and found Omar's science project folder. Empty. Due tomorrow.
"Omar," she called. "Didn't you tell Mama you finished the project on Tuesday?"
He appeared in the doorway, too fast. "I did. The file got deleted."
"Deleted how?"
"The laptop crashed. Or... you probably deleted it when you were printing all your stuff."
Layla folded her arms. "I haven't printed anything since Sunday."
"Then someone else did. Why are you always checking my things?"
His ears were bright red. His voice had gone high, the way it did when he was little and swore he hadn't eaten the dates.
Layla didn't shout. She just said, "Omar, it's okay to be behind. It's not okay to blame me."
He stood there, mouth open, a third lie ready, and suddenly too tired to say it.

qa.q: What did Layla find in Omar's project folder?
qa.a: The folder was empty, and the project was due tomorrow.

qa.q: What do Omar's red ears and high voice suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Omar felt panicked and ashamed, grabbing for new lies instead of admitting he hadn't done it.

qa.q: What could Omar do right now?
qa.a: Admit the project isn't done, apologise to Layla for blaming her, and tell Mama tonight so he can ask for help or more time.

qa.q: How did Layla handle being blamed?
qa.a: Layla stayed calm, didn't shout, and separated being behind, which is okay, from blaming her, which is not.

grounding: Shows a teenager caught in a lie inventing new excuses and turning on his sister, pushed by shame toward escape instead of admission.

passage:
In the Class 11 staffroom, Ritu ma'am laid two English essays side by side. The same three unusual phrases, the same spelling mistake in "necessary".
"Zainab, can you explain this?"
Zainab's throat closed. She had copied the last two paragraphs from Farah's notebook at 7 am on the bus. "Farah copied from me," she said.
"Farah submitted hers yesterday. Yours came in today."
"Then... I wrote it first in rough. She saw it at lunch." Zainab heard her own voice getting louder. "You always believe her because she's a topper!"
Ritu ma'am didn't raise her voice. "I'm not calling anyone a cheat yet. I'm asking what happened."
The fan clicked above them. Zainab stared at the misspelt word. Each new story needed another to hold it up, and she could feel the whole pile wobbling.
"Can I... sit down?" she whispered.

qa.q: Which word was misspelt the same way in both essays?
qa.a: 'Necessary'.

qa.q: Why did Zainab accuse Ritu ma'am of favouring Farah?
qa.a: Zainab panicked and felt ashamed, so attacking the teacher felt safer than admitting the copying.

qa.q: What would help Zainab now?
qa.a: Sit down, tell Ritu ma'am plainly that the last two paragraphs were copied, and apologise to Farah for blaming her.

qa.q: How might Farah be affected if Zainab's story had been believed?
qa.a: Farah would have been treated as a cheat for her own work, which shows how doubling down harms others too.

grounding: Shows a teenager caught copying adding lies and attacking the teacher, as shame pushes her toward escape rather than admission.

passage:
Dear Sonali,

I owe you the real version of Saturday, so here it is.

I said I had fever and couldn't come to your birthday. That was the first lie. The truth is my cousin had spare tickets to the kabaddi match, and I went.

When you showed me the photo on Monday, my face went hot and my brain just ran. I said the photo was from last year. Then, when you pointed at the date on the banner, I said you were checking up on me like a detective, and I walked off.

You didn't deserve that. You noticed something true, and I made you the problem, because owning up felt like shrinking in front of the whole class.

I'm sorry for skipping, sorry for the second story, and sorriest for turning on you. If you want to talk, I'll be on the library steps at lunch tomorrow.

Anjali

qa.q: What reason did Anjali first give for missing Sonali's birthday?
qa.a: Anjali said they had fever and couldn't come to the birthday.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when Sonali showed the photo, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anjali felt panicked and ashamed: their face went hot, their brain just ran, and owning up felt like shrinking in front of the whole class.

qa.q: What could Anjali try the next time a lie is found out?
qa.a: Take one breath and admit the first lie straight away, instead of adding a second story or turning on the person who noticed.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when called a detective?
qa.a: Sonali was probably hurt twice: first by the skipped birthday, then by being blamed for noticing something true.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, once caught, adds a second lie and attacks the person who noticed, because shame makes escape feel easier than admitting it.
